title: Theorem
body_md:
(Main theorem: a Rough Version)
    Given $\kappa \in (0,\frac23]$, $(\lambda_0,\lambda_1) \in \mathbb{R}^+ \times (0,1)$, there exists an open set of spherically symmetric initial data supported in $B(0,\lambda_0)$ with initial expanding rate $\lambda_1$ and initial mass $\delta^\frac1\kappa \ll 1$ in a suitable high-order weighted Sobolev space which lead to future-global solutions to the system \eqref{eq:RE}, \eqref{def: moving domain Omega_t}--\eqref{fallout rate}. Moreover, the support of these solutions expands linearly (with respect to an Eulerian observer) in time with an asymptotic rate $\bar\lambda \sim \lambda_1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
All estimates except for \eqref{est:ptlamt} and \eqref{est:difflamt} were proved in \cite[Lemma 2.1]{hadvzic2019class}. To prove \eqref{est:ptlamt}, we note that
    $$
    \partial_\tau \left(\frac{\partial_\tau\lambda}{\lambda}\right) = \lambda \partial_t^2\lambda = \delta\lambda^{-3\kappa},
    $$
    where we used the ODE for $\lambda$. Then the estimate follows immediately from \eqref{est:lambdaasym}.

    To prove \eqref{est:difflamt}, we note from the definition of $\tau$ and \eqref{lambdaasymp} that
    $$
    \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}- \bar\lambda = \partial_t \lambda- \bar\lambda = \partial_t a^\delta,
    $$
    which converges to $0$ thanks to the integrable decay bound $|\partial_t^2 a^\delta| \le C\delta (1+t)^{-3\kappa-1}$ when $\kappa > 0$. Moreover,
    $$
    |\bar{\lambda}_{\tau}^\delta - \bar\lambda^\delta| \le \int_\tau^\infty |\partial_t^2 a^\delta(t(\tilde\tau))|\lambda(\tilde \tau) d\tilde\tau \lesssim \delta \int_\tau^\infty e^{-3\kappa\bar\lambda^\delta \tilde\tau} d\tilde\tau \lesssim \frac{1}{\kappa\bar\lambda^\delta}\delta e^{-3\kappa\lambda^\delta \tau},
    $$
    which concludes the proof of \eqref{est:difflamt}.

\label{def: inner product}
    Given $i \in \mathbb{N}$, $\kappa > 0$, and $w$ an admissible weight (cf. Definition \ref{def: w}), we define the spaces $L^2_{\kappa,i}$ as the completion of $C^\infty_c(0,1)$ by the norm $\|\cdot\|_{\kappa,i}$ afforded by the following inner product:

title: Proof
body_md:
We recall 
        $
        \mathcal{F} = \left(\frac{\eta}{\zeta}\right)^2 \partial_{\zeta} \eta. 
        $
        Since $\eta = \Theta+\zeta$, 
        $$
        \mathcal{F} -1 = D_{\zeta}\Theta +\left(\frac{2\Theta}{\zeta}\partial_{\zeta} \Theta +\frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta^2}\right)+\frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta^2}\partial_{\zeta} \Theta. 
        $$
        Here, 
        \begin{align*}
            \frac{2\Theta}{\zeta}\partial_{\zeta} \Theta +\frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta^2} = \partial_{\zeta}\left(\frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta}\right) + \frac{1}{\zeta}\frac{2\Theta^2}{\zeta} = D_{\zeta}\left(\frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta}\right),
        \end{align*}
        and
        \begin{align*}
            \frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta^2}\partial_{\zeta} \Theta = \frac{1}{3}\partial_{\zeta}\left(\frac{\Theta^3}{\zeta^2}\right) +\frac{2}{3}\frac{\Theta^3}{\zeta^3}=\frac{1}{3}D_{\zeta}\left(\frac{\Theta^3}{\zeta^2}\right). 
        \end{align*}

label: prop:buildingblock
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Throughout the proof, all constants might change from line to line.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item 
        Invoking the identity \eqref{eq:calF-1}, then
        \begin{align*}
            \bar P_i \mathcal{F} &= \bar P_i D_{\zeta} \Theta + \bar P_i D_{\zeta} \left(\frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta}\right) + \frac13\bar P_i D_{\zeta} \left(\frac{\Theta^3}{\zeta^2}\right)\\
            &= P_{i+1} \Theta + P_{i+1} \left(\frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta}\right) + \frac13 P_{i+1} \left(\frac{\Theta^3}{\zeta^2}\right),
        \end{align*}
        where $P_{i+1} := \bar P_i D_{\zeta} \in \mathcal{P}_i$. Then the desired identity \eqref{PbarF} follows from Lemma \ref{lem:Fnonlinear}. 
     

        \item We first prove \eqref{PbarU0}. To begin with, we note the following computations:
        \begin{equation}\label{pzU0}
        \begin{split}
        \partial_{\zeta} (U^0)^{-2} &= \partial_{\zeta}\left(1-(\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta + \zeta))^2\right)\\
        &= -2(\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta + \zeta))(\partial_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\partial_{\zeta}\Theta + 1))\\
        &= -2(\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\Theta)(\partial_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\partial_{\zeta}\Theta + 1)) - 2\bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\zeta(\partial_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\partial_{\zeta}\Theta) - 2\bar{\lambda}_{\tau}^2 \zeta\\
        &= -2 (\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\Theta)\left(D_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta - \frac{2}{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(D_{\zeta}\Theta - \frac2\zeta \Theta + 1)\right)\\
        &\quad -2\bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\zeta\left(D_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta - \frac{2}{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(D_{\zeta}\Theta - \frac2\zeta \Theta)\right) - 2\bar{\lambda}_{\tau}^2\zeta.
        \end{split}
        \end{equation}
        Writing $\bar P_i = P_{i-1}\partial_{\zeta}$, $P_{i-1} \in \mathcal{P}_{i-1}$, and applying Lemma \ref{lem:generalproductrule}, we arrive at
        \begin{align*}
            \bar P_i (U^0)^{-2} &= \sum_{\substack{A_{1,2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1+l_2 =i,\\l_1 \le i-1 }} c^{l_1,l_2}_i(A_1\partial_\tau \Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau} A_1\Theta)(A_2\partial_\tau\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau} A_2\Theta)\\
            &\quad + \sum_{\substack{B_{1,2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1+l_2 =i,\\l_1 \le i-1 }}\bar c^{l_1,l_2}_i (B_1 \zeta)(B_2\partial_\tau\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau} B_2\Theta) + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}^2 \bar P_{i}\zeta^2\\
            &= \sum_{\substack{A_{1,2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1+l_2 =i,\\l_1 \le i-1 }} c^{l_1,l_2}_i(A_1\partial_\tau \Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau} A_1(\Theta+\zeta))(A_2\partial_\tau\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau} A_2\Theta) - \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}^2 \bar P_{i}\zeta^2,
        \end{align*}
        which completes the proof of \eqref{PbarU0} after we expand the expression above.
        
        To prove \eqref{PbarU0highest}, we view $\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{i+1} = \mathcal{D}_i\partial_{\zeta}$. According to the second line of \eqref{pzU0}, most terms can be treated in the same way as the proof of \eqref{PbarU0} except for the following top order term:
        \begin{align*}
        -2\mathcal{D}_{i}&\left[(\partial_{\tau} \Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta + \zeta))(\partial_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta)\right] = -2\mathcal{D}_i\left[(\partial_{\tau} \Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta + \zeta))(D_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta-\frac{2}{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta)\right]\\
        &= -2\mathcal{D}_i\left((\partial_{\tau} \Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta + \zeta)) D_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta - 2\frac{(\partial_{\tau}\Theta)^2}{\zeta} - 2\bar{\lambda}_{\tau} \left(1+\frac{\Theta}{\zeta}\right)\partial_{\tau}\Theta\right)\\
        &=: -2(I_1 + I_2 + I_3).
        \end{align*}
        Using Lemma \ref{lem:highestspatial}, we can write $I_1$ as
        \begin{align*}
            I_1 &= (\partial_{\tau} \Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta + \zeta))\mathcal{D}_{i+1}\partial_{\tau}\Theta + \sum_{\substack{A_{l_1,l_2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1 + l_2 = i+1,\\l_1,l_2 \le i}} c_i^{l_1,l_2}(A_1\partial_{\tau}\Theta)(A_2\partial_{\tau}\Theta)\\
            &\quad + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\sum_{\substack{A_{l_1,l_2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1 + l_2 = i+1,\\l_1,l_2 \le i}} c_i^{l_1,l_2} (A_1\Theta)(A_2\partial_{\tau}\Theta) + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\sum_{\substack{A_{l_1,l_2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1 + l_2 = i+1,\\l_1,l_2 \le i}} c_i^{l_1,l_2} (A_1\zeta)(A_2\partial_{\tau}\Theta)
        \end{align*}
        Using product rule \ref{eq:thetasquare}, we can write $I_2$ as
        $$
        I_2 = \sum_{\substack{A_{l_1,l_2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1 + l_2 = i+1,\\l_1,l_2 \le i}} c_i^{l_1,l_2}(A_1\partial_{\tau}\Theta)(A_2\partial_{\tau}\Theta).
        $$
        Finally using \eqref{Pproduct}, we can write $I_3$ as
        $$
        I_3 = \bar{\lambda}_{\tau} \sum_{\substack{A_{l_1,l_2}\in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1 + l_2 = i+1,\\l_2 \le i}}c_i^{l_1,l_2}(A_1\Theta)(A_2\partial_{\tau}\Theta).
        $$
        The identity \eqref{PbarU0highest} is thus proved by combining all computations above.
    \end{enumerate}

As we will see later, this exactly reflects the fact that the largest error appearing in energy estimates comes from low frequencies. We point out that this phenomenon is fundamentally tied to the scaling ansatz that we impose on the original variable $\rho$ and $u$, in the sense that the relativistic Euler equations \textbf{does not} admit any scaling symmetry in the original variables.

title: Proof
body_md:
We shall prove \eqref{U0k bd}--\eqref{smallness of calFGkk-1} in order. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textit{Proof of \eqref{U0k bd}.} This follows from \eqref{bootstrap U0} because, for each fixed $\bar\lambda$, we have $1 - \bar\lambda^2\zeta^2 \leq 1$, and it is also bounded away from $0$ since $\bar\lambda < 1$.

\item \textit{Proof of \eqref{bootstrap Theta}.} Since $0\leq j\leq 2$, from the Hardy-type embedding \eqref{est:LinftyHardy1} we conclude that $\|P_j \Theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C(\mathcal{E}^N(\tau))^{\frac12}$ for $j=0,1,2$, where $C>0$ is a constant independent of $M_*$ and $\epsilon'$. Now, by choosing $\epsilon'$ so that 
$$
M_*\epsilon \leq 10^{-4}C^{-2},\quad\text{whenever }\epsilon\leq \epsilon',
$$ 
we obtain \eqref{bootstrap Theta} from \eqref{bootstrap EN}. 

\item \textit{Proof of \eqref{bootstrap ptau Theta}.} Similar to the proof of \eqref{bootstrap Theta}, the estimate for $\|\partial_{\tau} \Theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}$ follows also from \eqref{bootstrap EN} and \eqref{est:LinftyHardy1}. To bound $\|\partial_{\tau}^2 \Theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}$, our strategy is to express $\partial_{\tau}^2 \Theta$ as a linear combination of terms involving at most one $\tau$-derivative of $\Theta$. From \eqref{eq:momlagmainfull}, we obtain
\begin{align}\label{pt2Theta bootstrap eq}
\begin{aligned}
    (1+\delta\lambda^{-3\kappa}w\mathcal{F}^{-\kappa}\mathcal{G}^{\kappa})\partial_{\tau}^2\Theta  =& -(1+\delta\lambda^{-3\kappa}w\mathcal{F}^{-\kappa}\mathcal{G}^{\kappa})\bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\partial_{\tau}\Theta-\delta\lambda^{-3\kappa}\bigg((1+\delta\lambda^{-3\kappa}w\mathcal{F}^{-\kappa}\mathcal{G}^{\kappa})\Theta\\
    &+(1+\kappa)\mathcal{F}^{-\kappa-2}\left(1+\frac{\Theta}{\zeta}\right)^4L_0\Theta
    + \sum_{j=1}^3\mathfrak{R}_j(\Theta) + \sum_{j=1}^6E_j\bigg).
    \end{aligned}
\end{align}
Now, by choosing $\epsilon'$ sufficiently small so that $\delta=\epsilon^{\frac12}< \frac{1}{100}$, we obtain from \eqref{bootstrap U0} and \eqref{bootstrap FG} that $(1+\delta\lambda^{-3\kappa}w\mathcal{F}^{-\kappa}\mathcal{G}^{\kappa})\approx 1$. 
In view of the definitions of $\mathfrak{R}_j(\Theta)$ \eqref{def:R1}--\eqref{def:R3} and $E_j$ \eqref{mainerror}, all terms on the RHS have at most one $\tau$--derivative on $\Theta$, apart from a term generated by $\delta\lambda^{-3\kappa}E_4$ when $\partial_{\tau}$ lands on $\mathcal{G}^{\kappa}$. 
However, this term can be absorbed by the LHS thanks to the smallness of $\delta$. Additionally, we infer from the first term on the RHS of \eqref{pt2Theta bootstrap eq}, whose coefficient is of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ size, that both $\|\partial_{\tau}^2\Theta\|_{L^{\infty}}$ and $\|\partial_{\tau}\Theta\|_{L^{\infty}}$ should be of $\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{-\frac32\kappa})$ size. 
This confirms the desired bound for $\|\partial_{\tau}^2\Theta\|_{L^{\infty}}$ in \eqref{bootstrap ptau Theta}. 
 

\item \textit{Proof of \eqref{est: induced bootstrap U^0}.} 
    Recall that $(U^0)^{-2} = 1-(\partial_\tau\Theta+\bar{\lambda}_{\tau} (\Theta+\zeta))^2$, we have
    $$
    \partial_{\tau} (U^0)^{-2} = -2 (\partial_\tau\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau} (\Theta+\zeta))\left(\partial_\tau^2\Theta + (\partial_{\tau}\bar{\lambda}_{\tau})(\Theta+\zeta) +\bar{\lambda}_{\tau}\partial_{\tau}\Theta\right),
    $$
and
    \begin{align*}
        \partial_{\zeta} (U^0)^{-2} = -2(\partial_\tau\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta+\zeta))\left(D_{\zeta}\partial_{\tau}\Theta+ \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(D_{\zeta}\Theta+3)\right) + 4\zeta^{-1}(\partial_\tau\Theta + \bar{\lambda}_{\tau}(\Theta+\zeta))^2. 
    \end{align*}
    These imply \eqref{est: induced bootstrap U^0} after invoking \eqref{est:lambdaasym}, \eqref{est:ptlamt}, \eqref{bootstrap Theta}, and \eqref{bootstrap ptau Theta}.  
    
\item  \textit{Proof of \eqref{est: induced bootstrap F}.} Recall that we have shown in Lemma \ref{lem:calF-1} that
    $$
    \mathcal{F}-1= D_{\zeta}\left(\Theta + \frac{\Theta^2}{\zeta}\right) + \frac13D_{\zeta}\left(\frac{\Theta^3}{\zeta^2}\right). 
    $$
    In light of Lemma \ref{lem:Fnonlinear}, this contributes to two types of terms:
    \begin{align*}
        D_{\zeta} \Theta, \quad \prod_{\substack{A_j\in \mathcal{P}_{l_j},\,l_j\leq 1\\
        \sum_{j=1}^{2 \text{ or } 3}l_j=2}}(A_j\Theta).
    \end{align*}
    Thus, both estimates in \eqref{est: induced bootstrap F} follow from \eqref{bootstrap Theta} and \eqref{bootstrap ptau Theta}, respectively, since $\partial_{\tau}^k\mathcal{F} = \partial_{\tau}^k(\mathcal{F}-1)$. 
    
\item    \textit{Proof of \eqref{est: induced bootstrap G}.} Since $\kappa \bar{\mathcal{G}} = \mathcal{G}^{-\kappa}$,  
    we have 
    $$
    |\partial_{\zeta} \mathcal{G}(\tau)|\leq \kappa^{-1}|G(\tau)^{\kappa+1}\partial_{\zeta}(\kappa\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\tau))|=\kappa^{-1}|\kappa^{-1}\bar{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}|^{\frac{1+\kappa}{\kappa}}|\partial_{\zeta}(\kappa\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\tau))|.
    $$
    Because \eqref{bootstrap FG} indicates that $|\kappa^{-1}\bar{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}|^{\frac{1+\kappa}{\kappa}} \approx 1$, hence it suffices to control $\|\partial_{\zeta} (\kappa\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\tau))\|_{L^{\infty}}$. We infer from Proposition \ref{prop:buildingblockpowersG}, \eqref{bootstrap FG}, \eqref{bootstrap Theta}, and \eqref{bootstrap ptau Theta} that $\|\partial_{\zeta} (\kappa\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\tau))\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq 10$. Additionally, $\|\partial_{\tau} \mathcal{G}(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq \frac{1}{10}\kappa^{-1}\lambda^{-\frac{3}{2}\kappa}$ follows from a similar argument together with \eqref{eq:dtbarcalG}, \eqref{bootstrap FG}, \eqref{est: induced bootstrap U^0}, and \eqref{est: induced bootstrap F}.  

\item \textit{Proof of \eqref{smallness of calFGkk-1}.} We infer from the Taylor expansion that 
$$
\mathcal{F}^{\kappa}-1 = \kappa(\mathcal{F}-1) + \mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{F}-1|^2). 
$$
Since $\|\mathcal{F}(\tau)-1\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq 10^{-2}$ from \eqref{bootstrap FG} and $\kappa<1$, $\|\mathcal{F}(\tau)^{\kappa}-1\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq \frac14$ follows. Additionally, $\|\mathcal{G}(\tau)^{\kappa}-1\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq \frac14$ is a direct consequence of \eqref{bootstrap FG} as $\frac{1}{\kappa}\bar{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}=\mathcal{G}^{\kappa}$.
\end{enumerate}

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fixing $i \le N+1$, we prove by inducting on $J := J_1 + J_2$. 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $J = 1$. We have either $J_1 = 1$ or $J_2 = 1$. In either case, \eqref{est:nonlinear} is reduced to
        \begin{equation}
            \label{nonlinaux1}
            \int_0^1 w^{\frac1\kappa + i}\zeta^2 |PH(\Theta)|^2d\zeta,
        \end{equation}
        where $P \in \mathcal{P}_{l}$, $l \le i$, and $H(\Theta) = \Theta$ or $\partial_{\tau}\Theta$. We first demonstrate the desired estimate for $H(\Theta) = \Theta$. If $l \le 4$, we invoke \eqref{est:LinftyHardy1} to bound \eqref{nonlinaux1} by $\|w^{\frac1\kappa + i}\|_{L^\infty} \|P\Theta\|_{L^\infty}^2 \lesssim \mathcal{E}^N$. If $l \ge 5$, we first consider $i \le N$. In this case, we invoke the $L^2$ embedding \eqref{est:L2Hardy} to obtain       
        $$
        \eqref{nonlinaux1} \le \|w^{\frac{1}{\kappa}+i-(\frac1\kappa + 2l - N)}\|_{L^\infty} \int_0^1 w^{\frac1\kappa + 2l - N}|P\Theta|^2 d\zeta \lesssim \mathcal{E}^N,
        $$
        where we used the fact that for $l \le i \le N$:
        $$
        \frac{1}{\kappa}+i-(\frac1\kappa + 2l - N) \ge N- i \ge 0.
        $$
For the reader's convenience, we verify here the applicability of \eqref{est:L2Hardy}. It requires
$\frac{N-\alpha}{2} \le k \equiv l \le N$, $P_k \in \mathcal{P}_k$. Since $N = \lfloor \frac1\kappa\rfloor + 10$, we have
$ l \equiv k  \geq \frac{N}{2} - \frac{\alpha}{2} = \frac{1}{2}(N - \frac{1}{\kappa})  = \frac{1}{2}( \lfloor \frac1\kappa\rfloor + 10 - \frac{1}{\kappa} )
        \geq \frac{9}{2}
$.
                                                  
        
        If $i = N+1$, we use \eqref{est:L2Hardy2} instead of \eqref{est:L2Hardy} to obtain
        $$
        \eqref{nonlinaux1} \le \|w^{\frac{1}{\kappa}+i-(\frac1\kappa + 2(l-1)+1 - N)}\|_{L^\infty} \int_0^1 w^{\frac1\kappa + 2(l-1)+1 - N}|P\Theta|^2 d\zeta \lesssim \mathcal{E}^N,
        $$
        where we used that
        $$
        \frac{1}{\kappa}+i-(\frac1\kappa + 2(l-1)+1 - N) \ge -i+1+N \ge 0.
        $$
        The scenario where $H(\Theta) = \partial_{\tau}\Theta$ is similar, where we only need to consider $i \le N$ due to the assumption of the lemma on the maximum number of derivatives falling on $\partial_{\tau}\Theta$. This ends the proof of the base case.
        
        \item $J \ge 2$. 
        We proceed by assuming the inductive hypothesis that \eqref{est:nonlinear} holds up to $J-1$. 
        Let us also without loss assume that $a_1 \le \hdots \le a_{J_1}$, $b_1 \le \hdots \le b_{J_2}$. We discuss the following cases:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $\min\{a_1, b_1 + 1\} \le 4$: in this case, either $A_1 \in \mathcal{P}_l$ or $B_1P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_l$, where $l \le 4$. Without loss of generality, we assume $a_1$ is the minimum and $H_1(\Theta) = \Theta$. Then we may apply \eqref{est:LinftyHardy1} to $A_1H_1(\Theta)$ to obtain the bound:
            \begin{align*}
                \eqref{est:nonlinear} &\lesssim \mathcal{E}^N\cdot\int_0^1 w^{\frac1\kappa + i}\zeta^2 \prod_{\substack{A_k \in \mathcal{P}_{a_k},\\\sum_{k=2}^{J_1}a_k \le i_1}}(A_kH_k(\Theta))^2\cdot \prod_{\substack{B_k \in \bar{\mathcal{P}}_{b_k},\\\sum_{k=1}^{J_2}b_k \le i_2 -1}}(B_k P_1\Theta)^2 d\zeta\\
                &\lesssim (\delta \lambda^{-3\kappa})^K (\mathcal{E}^N)^{J_1 + J_2},
            \end{align*}
            where we used the induction hypothesis in the final inequality above.
            \item $\min\{a_1, b_1 + 1\} \ge 5$: we consider $\max\{a_{J_1}, b_{J_2}\}$. Then by definition of $a_k, b_k$, it is clear that the maximum, and thus all $a_k, b_k$, are less or equal to $N - 4$. We first consider the case where $b_{J_2} = \max\{a_{J_1}, b_{J_2}\}$. Our plan is to bound $B_{{b_{J_2}}}P_1\Theta$ in $L^2$ using \eqref{est:L2Hardy} and all other terms using $L^\infty$ embedding \eqref{est:LinftyHardyweighted1N-4}. Indeed,
            \begin{align*}
                \eqref{est:nonlinear}&\lesssim \|w^{\frac1\kappa + i - (\frac1\kappa + 2b_{J_2}+ 2 - N)-2\sum_{k=1}^{J_2 - 1}(b_k - 1) - 2\sum_{l=1}^{J_1}(a_l - 2)}\|_{L^\infty}\\
                &\quad \times \prod_{\substack{A_k \in \mathcal{P}_{a_k},\\\sum_{k=1}^{J_1}a_k \le i_1}}\|w^{a_k - 2}A_kH_k(\Theta)\|_{L^\infty}^2 \cdot \prod_{\substack{B_k \in \bar{\mathcal{P}}_{b_k},\\\sum_{k=1}^{J_2-1}b_k \le i_2 -1}}\|w^{b_k - 1} B_kP_1\Theta\|_{L^\infty}^2\\
                &\quad \times \int_0^1 w^{\frac1\kappa + 2b_{J_2}+ 2 - N}\zeta^2 |B_{b_{J_2}}P_1\Theta|^2 d\zeta\\
                &\lesssim (\delta \lambda^{-3\kappa})^K (\mathcal{E}^N)^{J_1 + J_2},
            \end{align*}
            where we used that
            \begin{align*}
                \frac1\kappa + &i - (\frac1\kappa + 2b_{J_2}+ 2 - N)-2\sum_{k=1}^{J_2 - 1}(b_k - 1) - 2\sum_{l=1}^{J_1}(a_l - 2)\\
                &= i - 2(\sum_{k=1}^{J_1}a_k + \sum_{l=1}^{J_2}b_l) -2+N + 2(J_2 - 1) + 4J_1\\
                &\ge -i + N  + 2(J_1 + J_2) -2+2J_1 \ge 1+2J_1 > 0.
            \end{align*}
            Here, we used that $\sum a_k + \sum b_l \le i - 1$, $J_1 + J_2 \ge 2$, and $i \le N+1$.
            If $a_{J_1} = \max\{a_{J_1}, b_{J_2}\}$, we instead will bound $A_{{a_{J_1}}}H_{J_1}(\Theta)$ in $L^2$ using \eqref{est:L2Hardy} (or \eqref{est:L2Hardy2} when $i = N+1$) and all other terms using $L^\infty$ embedding \eqref{est:LinftyHardyweighted1N-4}. The argument follows similarly to the previous case and we omit the details here.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows from carefully translating the result in \cite{disconzi2022relativistic} to the variables used in our setting. Thus, here, we only highlight the main points. Interested readers can check Appendix \ref{S:Proof_of_LWP}, where a more detailed proof is given.

    Statement 1) follows from following the calculations of Section \ref{sect: setup} at the level of the data, whereas local existence and uniqueness of a classical solution to \eqref{eq:momlagmain} follows again by the procedure of Section \ref{sect: setup} applied to the Eulerian solution launched by the data $(\mathring{\rho},\mathring{u}^i)$. We note that our regularity assumptions are more than enough to justify the steps in Section \ref{sect: setup}.

    By \eqref{E:N_k_relation} and \eqref{E:Weighted_embedding_DIT}, we have $\Theta(\tau,\cdot) \in C^{N+2}([0,1])$. From this and the fact that such solutions satisfy the correct center-regularity conditions at $\zeta=0$ coming from spherical symmetry we obtain that their $\mathcal{X}^N$ norm is finite and thus their energy view of Remark \ref{R:Norm_equivalence_calX_calE}. This gives statement 2).

    Statement 3) follows from another judicious inspection of the procedure relating $(\mathring{\rho},\mathring{u}^i)$ to $(\Theta_0,U_0)$, but rephrased in terms of $(\mathring{\mathsf{r}},\mathring{\mathsf{v}}^i)$,  showing that this defines a map $(\mathring{\mathsf{r}},\mathring{\mathsf{v}}^i) \mapsto(\Theta_0,U_0)$ that is continuous relative to the $\mathcal{H}^{2k}_\text{ref}$ and $\mathcal{X}^N$ topologies. We note that the restriction to states of same mass singles out the correct set of perturbations in that spherically symmetric solutions to the relativistic Euler equations conserve mass.

    Finally, for statement 4), one verifies that under the corresponding bootstrap assumptions, we can invert back from the $(\Theta,\partial_\tau\Theta)$ variables to $(\rho,u^i)$ and then $(\mathsf{r},\mathsf{v}^i)$, with uniform control over the change of variables. The bound \eqref{E:Continuation_criterion_Lagrangian} then translate to uniform $C^2$ control of $(\mathsf{r},\mathsf{v}^i)$ over $[0,T^*)$, where $\tau^*$ and $T^*$ are related by $\tau^* = \int_0^{T^*} \frac{1}{\lambda(t)} dt$. Such control is enough to apply the continuation criterion of \cite{disconzi2022relativistic} and thus continue the solution $(\mathsf{r},\mathsf{v}^i)$ past $T^*$. Applying the procedure of Section \ref{sect: setup} to this continued-beyond-$T^*$ solution then gives a solution that continues $(\Theta,\partial_\tau\Theta)$ beyond $\tau^*$.

body_md:
\label{thm:mainprecise}
    Let $(\lambda_0,\lambda_1)\in \mathbb{R}^+\times (0,1)$ and $N\geq \lfloor\frac1\kappa\rfloor+10$. 
There exists $\epsilon_0=\epsilon_0(\kappa, N, \lambda_0, \lambda_1)$ such that for every $\epsilon\leq \epsilon_0$, $\delta\leq \epsilon$, and initial data $(\Theta_0, U_0)$ verifying 
    $$
    E^N(0) \leq \epsilon, 
    $$
    the associated solution to the equation \eqref{eq:momlagmain} from Theorem \ref{T:LWP},
    $$
    \tau \mapsto (\Theta(\tau,\cdot), \partial_{\tau}\Theta(\tau,\cdot))
    $$
    uniquely exists for all $\tau>0$. Moreover, there exists $M_*>0$, depending only on $\kappa, N, \lambda_0, \lambda_1$ such that 
    \begin{equation}\label{est: main theorem}
    E^N(\tau) \leq M_*\epsilon,\quad \tau>0. 
    \end{equation}
    Finally, there exists a $\tau$-independent attractor $\Theta_{\infty}$ such that
    \begin{equation}\label{convergence: main theorem}
    \sum_{j=0}^N \|\mathcal{D}_j \Theta(\tau,\cdot)-\mathcal{D}_j\Theta_{\infty}(\cdot)\|_j \rightarrow 0,
    \end{equation}
    as $\tau\to\infty$.

    \begin{align*}
        \bar P(fg) &= P(\partial_{\zeta} f g + f\partial_{\zeta} g) =P\left(D_{\zeta} fg + fD_{\zeta} g - \frac{4f}{\zeta}\cdot g\right)\\
        &= \sum_{\substack{A_{1,2} \in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1 + l_2 = i}}\bar{c}^{l_1,l_2}(A_1 f)(A_2 g),

\label{lem:highestspatial}
    The following identity holds:
    $$
\mathcal{D}_i(fD_{\zeta} g) = f\mathcal{D}_{i+1}g + \sum_{\substack{A_{1,2} \in \mathcal{P}_{l_1,l_2},\\l_1+l_2 = i+1,\\l_1, l_2 \le i}}c^{A_1A_2} (A_1f)(A_2g),

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove by induction. If $i = 1$, we see that
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal{D}_1 (fD_{\zeta} g) = D_{\zeta} (fD_{\zeta} g) = D_{\zeta} f D_{\zeta} g + f \mathcal{D}_2 g = \mathcal{D}_1 f\mathcal{D}_1 g + f \mathcal{D}_2 g,
    \end{align*}
    and we are done.

    To complete the inductive step, we assume $i$ is even. Then $\mathcal{D}_{i+1} = D_{\zeta} \mathcal{D}_{i}$, and we have
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal{D}_{i+1} (fD_{\zeta} g) &= D_{\zeta}\left(f\mathcal{D}_{i+1}g + \sum_{k \ge 1,A \in \mathcal{P}_k,B\in\mathcal{P}_{i-k+1}}^{i} (Af)(Bg)\right)\\
        &= \mathcal{D}_1 f \mathcal{D}_{i+1}g + f\mathcal{D}_{i+2}g + D_{\zeta} \left(\sum_{k \ge 1,A \in \mathcal{P}_k,B\in\mathcal{P}_{i-k+1}}^{i} (Af)(Bg)\right).
    \end{align*}
    Since $i+1$ is odd, then $k$ and $i-k+1$ have different parity. We may without loss assume that $k$ is even and hence $i-k+1$ is odd. Then
    $$
    D_{\zeta} ((Af)(Bg) ) = D_{\zeta} (Af) (Bg) + Af \partial_{\zeta}(Bg) = \mathcal{A} f Bg + Af\mathcal{B}g,
    $$
    where $\mathcal{A}\in \mathcal{P}_{k+1}$, $\mathcal{B} \in \mathcal{P}_{i-k+2}$. Thus we conclude the proof for $i$ even case. The case where $i$ is odd is similar.

label: lem:leadingorder
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove by induction. It is clear that \eqref{eq: leading order symmetry} is true for $i=1$ since $\mathcal{D}_1 = D_{\zeta}$. Suppose that \eqref{eq: leading order symmetry} holds for all $i\leq \ell$. We will show that it is true for $i=\ell+1$. 
   
   When $\ell$ is even, then $\mathcal{D}_{\ell+1} = D_{\zeta} \mathcal{D}_{\ell}$ or $\frac{1}{\zeta}\mathcal{D}_{\ell}$. From the inductive hypothesis, it suffices to show that $D_{\zeta}((\mathcal{D}_\ell f) g)$, $\frac{1}{\zeta}(\mathcal{D}_\ell f) g$, as well as $D_{\zeta}((Af)(Bg))$, $\frac{1}{\zeta}(Af)(Bg)$, with $A\in \mathcal{P}_k$ and $B\in \bar\mathcal{P}_{\ell-k}$, are of the correct form. The first two are easy to handle:
    $$
    D_{\zeta}((\mathcal{D}_\ell f) g) = (D_{\zeta}\mathcal{D}_\ell f)g + (\mathcal{D}_\ell f)(\partial_{\zeta} g),
    $$
    and
    $$
    \frac{1}{\zeta}(\mathcal{D}_\ell f) g = \left(\frac{1}{\zeta}\mathcal{D}_\ell f\right) g.
    $$
    Additionally, if $k$ is even, then $\ell-k$ is even. Thus, we can write
    $$
    D_{\zeta}((Af)(Bg)) = (D_{\zeta} A f)(Bg) + (Af)(\partial_{\zeta} Bg),  
    $$
    and 
    $$
    \frac{1}{\zeta}(Af)(Bg) =\left(\frac{1}{\zeta} Af\right) (Bg). 
    $$
   We note that both $D_{\zeta} A$ and $\frac{1}{\zeta} A\in \mathcal{P}_{k+1}$ with $k+1\leq \ell$. If $k$ is odd, then $\ell-k$ is odd. Thus, we can write
        $$
    D_{\zeta}((Af)(Bg)) = (\partial_{\zeta} A f)(Bg) + (Af)(D_{\zeta} Bg). 
    $$
    and 
    $$
    \frac{1}{\zeta}(Af)(Bg) = (Af)\left(\frac{1}{\zeta}Bg\right). 
    $$
  Here,  $\partial_{\zeta} A\in \mathcal{P}_{k+1}$ with $k+1\leq \ell$. 
    This completes the induction when $\ell$ is even. 

Let us assume $\ell$ is odd now. In this case, $\mathcal{D}_{\ell+1} = \partial_{\zeta} \mathcal{D}_{\ell}$. Hence, we need to show that $\partial_{\zeta}((\mathcal{D}_\ell f) g)$ as well as $\partial_{\zeta}((Af)(Bg))$ with $A\in \mathcal{P}_k$ and $B\in \bar\mathcal{P}_{\ell-k}$, are of the correct form. Note that
$$
\partial_{\zeta}((\mathcal{D}_\ell f) g)  = (\partial_{\zeta} \mathcal{D}_\ell f)g + (\mathcal{D}_{\ell} f)(\partial_{\zeta} g), 
$$
where $\partial_{\zeta} \mathcal{D}_\ell = \mathcal{D}_{\ell+1}$. As before, we consider $k$ is even and odd separately to justify if $\partial_{\zeta}((Af)(Bg))$ is of the correct form. If $k$ is even, then $\ell-k$ is odd. We write
$$
\partial_{\zeta}((Af)(Bg)) = (D_{\zeta} Af)(Bf) + (Af)(D_{\zeta} Bf) - (Af)\left(\frac{4}{\zeta}B g\right),
$$
where $D_{\zeta} A\in\mathcal{P}_{k+1}$ with $k+1\leq\ell$. 
If $k$ is odd, then $\ell-k$ is even. 
We write
$$
\partial_{\zeta}((Af)(Bg)) = (\partial_{\zeta} Af)(Bg)+ (Af)(\partial_{\zeta} Bg). 
$$
This completes the proof since $\partial_{\zeta} A\in \mathcal{P}_{k+1}$.

We prove this lemma here since the proof proceeds slightly differently from that of Lemma C.5 of \cite{guo2021continued}. We first prove \eqref{est:LinftyHardyweighted1N-4}. Fix $k \le N-4$ and $P_{k+2} \in \mathcal{P}_{k+2}$. Invoking \eqref{est:Linftyu} with $u = w^k P_{k+2}\Theta$ and $m = 3 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \|w^k P_{k+2}\Theta\|_{L^\infty} &\lesssim \sum_{i=1}^2 \int_0^\frac34 |B_i(w^k P_{k+2}\Theta)|^2 r^2dr\\
        &\quad+ \sum_{i = 0}^{4 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k} \int_\frac14^1 w^{\alpha - \lfloor\alpha\rfloor + 2(3 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k)}|B_i(w^k P_{k+2}\Theta)| r^2 dr.

    We also let $B_i = \mathcal{D}_i$ for $k$ even or $B_i = \bar{\mathcal{D}}_i$ for $k$ odd. To treat the first sum, we invoke the product rule \eqref{Pproduct} (or \eqref{Pbarproduct}) to deduce that
    $$
    B_i(w^k P_{k+2}\Theta) = \sum_{j=0}^i\sum_{A_1 \in \bar{\mathcal{P}}_j, A_2 \in \mathcal{P}_{k+2+i-j}} c_{jk}A_1(w^k)A_2\Theta.
    $$
    By the chain rule \eqref{eq:chainrule} as well as Lemma \ref{lem:wderivative}, we know that $A_1(w^k)$ is a smooth function near $\zeta = 0$, and thus $|A_1(w^k)| \lesssim 1$. Since $k+2 + i \le k+4 \le N$, we conclude that the first sum is controlled by $\mathcal{E}^N$ after using \eqref{est:Dicoercivity}. 

    As for the second sum, a similar reasoning to above would yield 
    \begin{align*}
        &\sum_{i = 0}^{4 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k} \int_\frac14^1 w^{\alpha - \lfloor\alpha\rfloor + 2(3 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k)}|B_i(w^k P_{k+2}\Theta)| r^2 dr \\
        &\lesssim \sum_{i = 0}^{4 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k}\sum_{j=0}^i\sum_{A_1 \in \bar{\mathcal{P}}_j, A_2 \in \mathcal{P}_{k+2+i-j}} \int_\frac14^1 w^{\alpha - \lfloor\alpha\rfloor + 2(3 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k)} |A_1(w^k)A_2\Theta|^2r^2 dr\\
        &\lesssim \sum_{i = 0}^{4 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k}\sum_{j=0}^i\sum_{A_2 \in \mathcal{P}_{k+2+i-j}} \int_\frac14^1 w^{\alpha - \lfloor\alpha\rfloor + 2(3 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k)} w^{2k-2j}|A_2\Theta|^2r^2 dr\\
        &\lesssim \sum_{i = 0}^{4 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k}\sum_{j=0}^i\sum_{A_2 \in \mathcal{P}_{k+2+i-j}} \int_\frac14^1 w^{\alpha + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor + 6-2j} |A_2\Theta|^2r^2 dr
    \end{align*}
    where we used the chain rule and Lemma \ref{lem:wderivative} in the second to the last inequality. Now, note that $w^{\alpha + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor + 6-2j} \lesssim w^{\alpha + k + 2 + i-j}$ since $j \le i \le 4 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor - k$. Moreover, the term which contains the most derivatives have $k + 2 + i \le 6 + \lfloor\alpha\rfloor \le N$ derivatives. We thus conclude that the second sum is also bounded by $\mathcal{E}^N$ after using \eqref{est:Dicoercivity}. The bound for $\delta^{-1}\lambda^{-3\kappa}\|w^kP_{k+2}\partial_{\tau}\Theta \|_{L^\infty}^2$ is similar. 

    The proof for other inequalities follow from similar arguments, where the proof for \eqref{est:LinftyHardyweighted1N-3} and \eqref{est:LinftyHardyweighted2N-4} utilizes \eqref{est:Linftyur} in place of \eqref{est:Linftyu}.
